about

I'm a senior at Tufts studying applied physics, drawn to mechanical design, hardware testing, and data. The three projects here are where I found each of those threads.

Outside of work, I'm general manager at WMFO (Tufts Freeform Radio), I play guitar, and I chase down as many concerts as I can. I grew up in Portland, Oregon, so backpacking, camping, and snowboarding are non‑negotiable. I'm currently looking for post‑grad roles that let me keep both the technical and outdoor sides of that curiosity alive.

sheet 01

Assistive device for self‑administering eye drops

task
Mechanically test a prototype assistive device for administering eye drops.
result
Built a custom test apparatus that measured the force needed to dispense drops, feeding a clinical study behind a patent application.

With Professor Gary Leisk at Bray Labs, in partnership with Lahey Clinic, I helped test an assistive device designed to reduce the force and aiming precision that eye drops demand — aimed at elderly glaucoma patients with dexterity challenges.

Working alongside a team of graduate students and ophthalmologist Dr. David Ramsey, I designed and 3D-printed test fixtures, fabricated a sheet-metal bracket in the machine shop, and logged force measurements in Excel. The mechanical data ran alongside usability surveys at Lahey Clinic, both feeding into a larger study supporting the device's patent application.

sheet 02

Modeling ocean turbulence at Oregon State

task
Design an ocean turbulence model and answer a self-formed research question using large-eddy simulations.
result
Produced simulation results on Langmuir turbulence's effect on vertical mixing, presented at a department symposium and written into a manuscript.

As an NSF REU researcher with Dr. Amrapalli Garanaik at Oregon State, I built my own ocean turbulence model in Oceananigans.jl — an open-source Large Eddy Simulation framework written in Julia — and ran simulations exploring how Langmuir turbulence affects vertical mixing.

Along the way I learned to trace and modify high-level Julia code, interpret complex simulation output into clear plots and figures, version my models on GitHub, and run longer, computationally expensive simulations on HPC clusters via the command line and Slurm Workload Manager.

sheet 03

Heat transfer FEA for a laser baseplate

task
Design, machine, and thermally validate a baseplate for a holographic laser to a fixed external spec.
result
Delivered a machined aluminum baseplate plus an FEA thermal model

For my Materials and Manufacturing final project, my team designed a baseplate for a holographic laser in SolidWorks, cut it from aluminum on a waterjet in the Bray Machine Shop, and ran FEA thermal tests simulating heat transfer from the mounted laser.

The plate had to match specifications from an online build blog for the laser itself, which sharpened my CAD skills for working to a fixed spec, and building the FEA model with matching initial conditions gave me hands-on grounding in heat transfer fundamentals.
